passage:
Dear Diary,
Monday was chess club: I lost twice and yawned. Tuesday was dance with Usha, which was fun but my feet got tangled. Today Masi gave me an old camera with no film, only a screen. I took 43 photos of ants carrying a crumb across the balcony. I forgot to eat my snack! Usha called and I missed it 😅. When I looked at the clock, a whole hour was gone and I didn't even notice. Mummy said, "You were so still, Hansa, I thought you were asleep." I'm not sure if I want to be a photographer or an ant scientist. Maybe both? Tomorrow I'm going to try the camera on the pigeons.

qa.q: How many photos did Hansa take of the ants?
qa.a: Hansa took 43 photos of ants carrying a crumb across the balcony.

qa.q: What does losing a whole hour suggest Hansa felt about the camera compared with chess or dance?
qa.a: Hansa felt absorbed and delighted: Hansa forgot the snack, missed Usha's call and lost a whole hour, while chess only brought yawns.

qa.q: How could Hansa's mother support this new interest?
qa.a: She could let Hansa keep experimenting with the camera and ask to see Hansa's favourite photos, without pushing a career choice yet.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about the missed call?
qa.a: Usha may feel a little ignored at first, but if Hansa explains and shares the ant photos, Usha may find it funny and interesting.

grounding: It shows a child trying several activities and noticing which one makes the hours slip by unnoticed.

passage: In the kasba, Salma's father runs a small cycle-repair shop beside the bus stand. Chandrika, Salma's friend from Class 6, started coming after school to wait for her bus. At first she only sat on the tyre pile, bored. Then one day a boy's chain slipped, and Salma's father was busy. Chandrika picked up a spanner. "Show me?" Salma laughed, but her father nodded. Chandrika watched how he hooked the chain back, then did the next one herself, grease up to her wrists. After that she missed two buses in a week. At home her mother scolded her for her black nails. Chandrika only said, "Amma, I want to learn how the gears work."

qa.q: Where is Salma's father's shop?
qa.a: It is beside the bus stand in the kasba.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika miss two buses in a week?
qa.a: She was so absorbed in fixing the cycles that she lost track of time; the repair work had caught her interest in a way sitting on the tyre pile never did.

qa.q: How could Chandrika's mother respond to this new interest?
qa.a: Instead of only scolding about her nails, she could ask what she is learning and help her plan her time so she doesn't miss the bus.

qa.q: How does Salma's father seem to see Chandrika's interest?
qa.a: He takes it seriously, nodding and letting her try, which suggests he respects her wish to learn even though she is a young girl in his shop.

grounding: It shows a child discovering an absorbing hobby through trying a new activity in a small town.

passage: Tariq's mum signed him up for a Saturday taster day at the community centre in Rotterdam. Four stations, twenty minutes each. At football, Tariq kept glancing at the clock. At drawing, he sketched one lopsided boat and stopped. At cooking, he and Alejandro, a boy he'd just met, burned the pancakes and laughed. The last station was a small electronics table with buzzers and wires. Tariq made a bulb light up, then made it blink. The leader called time, and Tariq didn't hear her. Alejandro had to tap his shoulder. On the tram home, Tariq kept drawing circuits on the steamed-up window. "Can I go back next week?" he asked. "Just to the wires."

qa.q: What did Tariq and Alejandro burn at the cooking station?
qa.a: They burned the pancakes.

qa.q: What does Tariq not hearing the leader call time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was completely absorbed and excited by the electronics, far more than at the other stations where he watched the clock.

qa.q: What small step could Tariq's mum take to support this interest?
qa.a: She could find a regular beginner electronics group or simple kit so he can keep exploring it, while still letting him try other things.

qa.q: How might Alejandro remember the taster day differently from Tariq?
qa.a: For Alejandro the fun part may have been the burned pancakes and meeting Tariq, since each child finds different activities absorbing.

grounding: It shows a child trying many short activities and noticing which one holds his attention.

passage: The summer camp at the Rajkot community centre had a new room every day. Himani, eleven, tried everything: Monday she yawned through chess, Tuesday she tripped over her feet in dance, Wednesday the coding class made her head spin. On Thursday it was pottery. She pressed her thumbs into cold clay, and the wheel began to turn. The room noise faded. When Pallavi didi, the camp volunteer, rang the lunch bell, Himani didn't move. 'Himani? Lunch!' 'Two minutes. The side keeps flopping.' Twenty minutes later, her bowl was lopsided and her arms were grey to the elbow. 'You missed lunch,' Pallavi didi said. Himani looked surprised. 'Already? Can I come back tomorrow?'

qa.q: On which day did Himani try pottery?
qa.a: She tried pottery on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Himani feel at the pottery wheel, given she didn't hear the lunch bell?
qa.a: She felt completely absorbed and interested, more than in any other activity she tried, and was eager to come back the next day.

qa.q: How could Pallavi didi support what she noticed?
qa.a: She could tell Himani's family about her focus on clay and help her find more chances to try pottery.

qa.q: What would change if the camp had offered only one activity, like chess?
qa.a: Himani might never have discovered pottery and might have thought she wasn't good at anything.

grounding: Shows a child trying many activities and noticing what absorbs her attention.

passage: I'm Zubin, and Ritu sits next to me in class six. This year she's joined everything. In June it was karate; she quit after two weeks. In July she said she'd learn the keyboard, and she did practise a few times. But here's what I keep noticing: whatever class it is, the back of her notebook fills up with comics. Little people with big heads, arguing about lunch. In the maths period she draws. In the bus she draws. Last week our teacher took the notebook, and I thought Ritu would cry. Instead Ma'am laughed and said, 'Make one for the school magazine.' Ritu hasn't talked about karate since. I don't know if she'll become an artist. But she never stops.

qa.q: What does Ritu draw at the back of her notebook?
qa.a: Comics of little people with big heads arguing about lunch.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling when the teacher took her notebook?
qa.a: She was probably scared of being in trouble, which is why Zubin thought she would cry.

qa.q: How could Ritu's family help her explore this interest?
qa.a: They could give her time and paper for comics while still letting her try other activities.

qa.q: Why might Zubin notice Ritu's drawing more than her karate?
qa.a: Zubin sees Ritu drawing everywhere, all the time, while the other activities came and went.

grounding: An observer notices a classmate trying many hobbies and returning again and again to one.

passage:
First week of June: Suraj, ten, joined the colony cricket camp. He spent most of the time picking grass in the outfield. “Boring,” he told his aunt Rekha.
Late June: Rekha took him to a drawing class. He drew a cat, then a car. It was fine. He kept looking at the clock.
Mid-July: At a clay workshop in the community hall, Suraj made a small elephant. Then a bowl. Then a dragon with tiny scales. When Rekha came to fetch him, the hall was nearly empty and his hands were grey to the wrists.
“Already?” he asked. “Can I come again tomorrow?”

qa.q: What did Suraj make at the clay workshop?
qa.a: A small elephant, a bowl and a dragon with tiny scales.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel at the clay workshop?
qa.a: He felt so absorbed and happy that he lost track of time and wanted to come back.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that helped Suraj find his interest?
qa.a: She let him try different activities until he found one that absorbed him.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel seeing Suraj's grey hands?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and amused that he has found something he loves.

grounding: Over several weeks a ten-year-old tries activities and notices what absorbs his attention.

passage:
Sarita, you want to know how I became an electrician? Let your Shalini Aaji tell you.
When I was eleven, in Nashik, my mother sent me to dance class. I tripped over my own feet. Then sewing. I pricked my fingers and cried.
But every evening my uncle, Dattu Kaka, sat on the verandah fixing radios. I would sit beside him, handing him screws. One day he let me hold the soldering iron. I didn't notice the sun go down. My mother had to call me three times for dinner.
People said girls don't fix radios. I didn't listen. Now look, forty years of wiring houses. Notice what makes you forget the time, Sarita.

qa.q: What was Dattu Kaka fixing on the verandah?
qa.a: He was fixing radios.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel when fixing radios with her uncle?
qa.a: She felt so absorbed and happy that she didn't notice the sun go down.

qa.q: What choice in the story shaped Shalini's future?
qa.a: Choosing to follow her interest in fixing radios, even when people said girls don't do that.

qa.q: How might Dattu Kaka have felt about young Shalini's interest?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased and proud to share his skill with her.

grounding: A grandmother tells how she discovered her lifelong interest by noticing what absorbed her.

passage:
Nazia, eleven, stood outside the music room after school every Thursday, listening to the guitar class. Her family couldn't afford the fees this year.
One day, the teacher, Mr Tenzin, came out. “You're always here. Do you play?”
“No, sir. I just like listening.”
He looked at her for a moment. “There's an old guitar in the storeroom with only five strings. You can practise on it after class. Free.”
The next Thursday, Nazia sat in the corner with the old guitar, pressing strings until her fingertips hurt. When Mr Tenzin switched off the lights, she was still trying to play the first four notes of a song.

qa.q: How many strings did the old guitar have?
qa.a: It had only five strings.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel practising on the old guitar?
qa.a: She felt absorbed and determined, practising until her fingertips hurt.

qa.q: What did Mr Tenzin do that helped Nazia explore her interest?
qa.a: He noticed her listening and offered her the old guitar to practise for free.

qa.q: How might Mr Tenzin feel seeing Nazia still practising when he switches off the lights?
qa.a: He probably feels touched and hopeful about her dedication.

grounding: Despite little money, an eleven-year-old finds a way to follow the music that absorbs her.

passage:
This year, Tenzin had tried everything in the Delhi school's activity week: chess, football, dance, painting.
Chess made him sleepy. Football made him tired. Dance made him laugh at himself.
Then came the clay modelling club. He sat down and started shaping a yak. When the bell rang, he looked up, surprised. An hour had gone.
"You didn't even hear the bell," said his sister Rashmi, who had come to pick him up.
Tenzin didn't answer. He was smoothing the yak's horns.
On the way home, he asked, "Can I go to clay club every week?"
Rashmi laughed. "You looked like nothing else existed."

qa.q: What did Tenzin shape in the clay club?
qa.a: A yak.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he looked up, surprised?
qa.a: Tenzin felt absorbed and happy, so lost in the clay that he didn't notice the time.

qa.q: How could Tenzin's family support this new interest?
qa.a: They could let him join the club regularly and keep some clay at home to practise.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see Tenzin at the clay club?
qa.a: Rashmi notices he is completely absorbed, as if nothing else existed.

grounding: A child tries many activities and notices one that deeply absorbs him.

passage:
"Kalyani! Dinner!" Chandrika called for the third time.
"Coming! Just one more screw."
Chandrika found her sister on the floor, surrounded by bits of Dadaji's old radio. "You've been at this for three hours."
"Really?" Kalyani blinked. "I thought it was twenty minutes."
"What are you even doing?"
"Look." Kalyani connected two wires. The radio crackled. Then music.
Chandrika stared. "How did you…?"
"I watched the repair man in the market last month. And I asked him questions."
"You never sit still for homework."
Kalyani grinned. "This isn't homework. This is fun."

qa.q: Whose old radio was Kalyani fixing?
qa.a: Dadaji's.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she said she thought it was twenty minutes?
qa.a: Kalyani felt surprised and absorbed, so into the radio that time flew.

qa.q: How could Chandrika or the family support Kalyani's interest?
qa.a: They could give her old gadgets to explore safely and find a class or mentor for electronics.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see Kalyani after the radio works?
qa.a: Chandrika is amazed and sees a new side of her sister who usually can't sit still.

grounding: A child discovers an absorbing interest in fixing a radio.

passage:
When I was eleven, I tried football and hated the shouting. I tried guitar and my fingers hurt. My uncle Santosh said, "Keep trying things. Something will grab you."
That winter he took me to the lake near Aizawl at dawn with his binoculars. I saw a small green bird with a red throat. I couldn't look away.
I made him wait an hour while I watched it. I drew it in my maths notebook when I got home.
After that, I kept a notebook of birds. I'm Lalremsiami, and I'm thirteen now. I want to study birds when I grow up. It started with that one morning.

qa.q: What did the bird Lalremsiami saw look like?
qa.a: A small green bird with a red throat.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when unable to look away from the bird?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt delighted and full of wonder, completely absorbed by the bird.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that helped Lalremsiami find an interest?
qa.a: He encouraged trying many things and took Lalremsiami somewhere new, which led to discovering bird-watching.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel waiting an hour at the lake?
qa.a: Santosh was probably patient and happy to see his advice working.

grounding: A young person recalls discovering a lasting interest in birds after trying many activities.

passage:
Summer activity club, week 4. Notes by Shankar, supervisor.
Afreen has tried everything we offer: chess (left after one game), dance (enthusiastic for two days), cricket (spent most of the time talking). I had started to wonder if nothing would hold her.
This week we put out clay. She sat at the pottery wheel on Tuesday and did not look up for an hour and a half. When the bell rang she said "already?" and asked to stay. Her pot collapsed three times; she laughed and started again each time. On Thursday she came early and asked the potter about glazes.
I have told her parents what I saw. My plan: give her a regular wheel slot, but keep other activities open. At nine she doesn't need to choose forever.

qa.q: How long did Afreen sit at the wheel on Tuesday without looking up?
qa.a: Afreen did not look up for an hour and a half.

qa.q: What does Afreen's laughing when her pot collapsed suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt absorbed and happy enough in the work that failure didn't discourage her.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen's parents after reading this note?
qa.a: Encourage the clay without turning it into pressure, and let her keep trying other things too.

qa.q: How might Shankar see the week compared with the first three?
qa.a: Shankar probably feels relieved and pleased, having seen for the first time what really holds Afreen's attention.

grounding: Illustrates, through a supervisor's note, a child trying many activities and one clearly absorbing her.

passage:
Makar Sankranti, 14 Jan
Diary, it's me, Parveen. Irfan Bhai said making a kite is boring, just buy one. I tried anyway. I cut the paper wrong twice. The third one worked!!
I forgot to eat lunch. Ammi had to call three times. I didn't even hear the neighbours' "kaipoche" shouts for ages because I was measuring the sticks.
Then it flew. Only for a little while before it went sideways into the neem tree, but it FLEW. Irfan said, "Okay, maybe not so boring."
Last month I tried the keyboard and gave up in a week. Painting too. This felt different. My hands wanted to keep going.
Tomorrow I'm going to try one with a longer tail. 🪁

qa.q: How many times did Parveen cut the paper wrong?
qa.a: Parveen cut the paper wrong twice.

qa.q: What does forgetting lunch suggest about how Parveen felt while making the kite?
qa.a: It suggests Parveen felt completely absorbed and excited, so deep in the work that hunger and noise faded.

qa.q: How could Ammi support this new interest?
qa.a: Ammi could give Parveen space and simple materials to keep building, without insisting it becomes a big hobby.

qa.q: How does Irfan see kite-making by the end of the day?
qa.a: Irfan seems a little impressed, admitting it's "maybe not so boring" once the kite flew.

grounding: Shows a child noticing, in a diary, that one activity absorbs attention in a way earlier ones didn't.

passage:
During the Pongal holidays in their village, Usha tried to do everything at once. She beat the thavil drum with her uncle until her wrists ached. She stirred the pongal pot till Paati shooed her away. She even tried milking the cow, which kicked the bucket over.
On the third morning, she sat on the step while her grandmother Lakshmi drew the kolam, white dots in rows, lines looping round them. "Can I try?"
Lakshmi gave her the rice flour. Usha's first lines wobbled. She wiped them and tried again. The sun got hot. Her cousins called her to play. She didn't hear.
When she finally looked up, half the courtyard was covered.
"You were gone somewhere," Lakshmi said, smiling.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi drawing on the third morning?
qa.a: Lakshmi was drawing the kolam, white dots in rows with lines looping round them.

qa.q: What does Usha not hearing her cousins suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests Usha was deeply absorbed and content, lost in the drawing.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi help Usha grow this interest?
qa.a: Lakshmi could keep giving her rice flour and teach her new patterns now and then, letting her practise at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel seeing Usha cover half the courtyard?
qa.a: Lakshmi probably feels proud and pleased that her granddaughter has found something she loves in a family tradition.

grounding: Illustrates a child trying many festival activities and noticing which one absorbs her attention.

passage:
It was July in Buenos Aires, cold and grey, and Mateo, ten, had tried everything that winter: football on Mondays, piano on Wednesdays, drawing class on Saturdays. He liked them. He forgot them the moment they ended.
Then one Sunday, his uncle Daniel brought an old radio that crackled. "Want to see inside?"
Mateo sat at the kitchen table for three hours without moving. He sorted tiny screws, cleaned a dusty dial with a cotton bud, asked question after question. When the radio finally played a tango, he jumped up and shouted.
His sister Lucía rolled her eyes. "You never shout at piano."
That night, Mateo asked if he could keep the screwdriver.

qa.q: How long did Mateo sit at the kitchen table?
qa.a: He sat for three hours without moving.

qa.q: What was Mateo feeling when the radio played a tango?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and proud, jumping up and shouting after hours of absorbed work.

qa.q: How could Mateo's family help him explore this new interest?
qa.a: They could let him keep the screwdriver, find old gadgets to open safely with an adult, and give him time with Daniel.

qa.q: What does Lucía notice about her brother that others might miss?
qa.a: Lucía notices he never gets this excited about piano, which hints that fixing things is what truly absorbs him.

grounding: Shows a child trying many activities and noticing which one completely holds his attention.
